### Problem: Kth Largest Element in a Stream {#sec-salgo-p4-b}

::: {.p-statement}

Design a class that, given $k$ and an initial array `nums` ($1 \le k \le \textit{nums.length}+1 \le 10^4$, scores in $[-10^4, 10^4]$), supports `add(val)` which inserts `val` into the running stream and **returns the $k$-th largest score so far** (with multiplicity). At most $10^4$ calls to `add`.

Source: [LC 703 · Kth Largest Element in a Stream](https://leetcode.com/problems/kth-largest-element-in-a-stream/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}

Example — `k=3, nums=[4,5,8,2]`, then `add(3)→4`, `add(5)→5`, `add(10)→5`, `add(9)→8`, `add(4)→8`.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
@sec-salgo-p4-a asked for top-$k$ of a batch you could see all at once. Here the data **arrives one value at a time**, so you may not re-scan the whole history per query. The fix is to keep a *state* that already answers the question: a min-heap holding exactly the $k$ largest scores seen. Its root is simultaneously the smallest of the top-$k$ and therefore the $k$-th largest overall — the answer is `heap[0]`, in $O(1)$, and each insert costs $O(\log k)$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Resort on every add.** Append `val`, sort the whole pool descending, return index $k-1$. Correct and obviously so — but $O(n \log n)$ per call, $O(n^2 \log n)$ across $n$ adds.
2. **Bounded min-heap of the top $k$.** Keep a min-heap of size $k$. On `add`: if the heap is under capacity push; else push only if `val` beats the root, popping the root. Return the root. $O(\log k)$ per add, $O(k)$ space.

**Invariant.** The heap contains the $k$ largest values seen so far; its minimum is the $k$-th largest, so it is the eviction threshold and the returned answer at the same time.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Resort on every add

::: {.form-next}
Keep the full pool; on each `add` append, sort descending, read index $k-1$. $O(n \log n)$ per call. It is the definition and the oracle for the heap.

**Worked example.** pool $[4,5,8,2]$; `add(3)` → sorted $[8,5,4,3,2]$, 3rd largest $=4$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("stream", "sort")
    assert str(final) == "[4, 5, 5, 8, 8]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
class KthLargest703Sort:
    def __init__(self, k, nums):
        self.k = k
        self.pool = list(nums)

    def add(self, val):
        self.pool.append(val)
        return sorted(self.pool, reverse=True)[self.k - 1]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// keep full pool, resort each add; O(n log n) per add
struct KthLargest703Sort {
    int k; vector<int> pool;
    KthLargest703Sort(int k, vector<int> nums) : k(k), pool(nums) {}
    int add(int val) {
        pool.push_back(val);
        vector<int> s = pool;
        sort(s.begin(), s.end(), greater<int>());
        return s[k - 1];
    }
};
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Every query re-derives the whole order from scratch. That is fine for a handful of adds and $10^4$ scores, but it is $O(n)$ memory and $O(n \log n)$ time *per call* — the exact waste the streaming setting is designed to expose.

#### Bounded min-heap of the top k

::: {.form-next}
Maintain a min-heap of exactly the $k$ largest values. Construction: heapify the pool, then trim to $k$ by popping the smallest extras. On `add(val)`: if the heap has room push; else if `val > root` replace the root. The answer is always the root. $O(\log k)$ per add, $O(k)$ space.

**Worked example.** $k=3$, pool $[4,5,8,2]$ → top-3 heap $\{4,5,8\}$ root 4. `add(3)`: $3\not>4$ → still 4. `add(5)`: evict 4 → $\{5,5,8\}$ root 5. `add(10)` → root stays 5. `add(9)` → evict 5 → $\{8,9,10\}$ root 8. `add(4)` → $4\not>8$ → root 8. Yields $[4,5,5,8,8]$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("stream", "heap")
    assert str(final) == "[4, 5, 5, 8, 8]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-salgo-703-heap
from heapq import heapify, heappush, heappop, heapreplace

class KthLargest703:
    def __init__(self, k, nums):
        self.k = k
        self.heap = list(nums)
        heapify(self.heap)
        while len(self.heap) > k:              # trim to the k largest
            heappop(self.heap)

    def add(self, val):
        if len(self.heap) < self.k:
            heappush(self.heap, val)
        elif val > self.heap[0]:
            heapreplace(self.heap, val)        # pop root, push val, in one O(log k) step
        return self.heap[0]

ops = KthLargest703(3, [4, 5, 8, 2])
assert [ops.add(v) for v in [3, 5, 10, 9, 4]] == [4, 5, 5, 8, 8]
ops2 = KthLargest703(4, [7, 7, 7, 7, 8, 3])
assert [ops2.add(v) for v in [2, 10, 9, 9]] == [7, 7, 7, 8]
for _ in range(300):                       # stress test against the resort-every-time oracle
    k = random.randint(1, 6)
    start = [random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(max(0, k - 1), 10))]
    fast, slow = KthLargest703(k, start), KthLargest703Sort(k, start)
    for _ in range(15):
        v = random.randint(-9, 9)
        assert fast.add(v) == slow.add(v)
print("KthLargest703 OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// min-heap of the k largest; root is the k-th largest
struct KthLargest703 {
    int k; priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> pq;   // min-heap
    KthLargest703(int k, vector<int> nums) : k(k) {
        for (int x : nums) { pq.push(x); if ((int)pq.size() > k) pq.pop(); }
    }
    int add(int val) {
        if ((int)pq.size() < k) pq.push(val);
        else if (val > pq.top()) { pq.pop(); pq.push(val); }
        return pq.top();
    }
};
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The min-heap keeps its *smallest* member on top — which, among the $k$ largest, is precisely the $k$-th largest. Construction heapifies the whole pool in $O(n)$ and then pops the smallest extras until only the $k$ largest remain. A new value only matters if it exceeds that top; `heapreplace` pops and pushes in a single $O(\log k)$ sift. The two LC examples are run verbatim as asserts, so a wrong heap policy fails the render.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Resort** is $O(n \log n)$ per `add`, $O(n)$ space. **Bounded heap** is $O(\log k)$ per `add` ($O(\textit{initial } n \log k)$ to build), $O(k)$ space — independent of how long the stream has run, which is the whole point.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Fewer than $k$ values so far: the C++/Python guard `size < k` pushes without evicting; the problem guarantees $k \le$ length $+ 1$ so the root exists once queried at capacity.
- Duplicates count: `val > top` (strict) means an equal value does *not* evict — matches "with multiplicity".
- $k = 1$: the heap degenerates to a running maximum.
:::
